title: Humility, Plato’s and ours
source_text: Εἶτα μετὰ ταῦτα ὁ Κέλσος ὡς περιηχηθεὶς τὰ περὶ ταπεινοφροσύνης καὶ μὴ ἐπιμελῶς αὐτὴν νοήσας βούλεται μὲν τὴν παρ᾿ ἡμῖν κακολογεῖν. οἴεται δ᾿ αὐτὴν παράκουσμα εἶναι τῶν Πλάτωνος λόγων, ὅς φησι ποὺ ἐν τοῖς Νόμοις· „ὁ μὲν δὴ θεὸς, ὥσπερ καὶ ὁ παλαιὸς λόγος, ἀρχήν τε καὶ τελευτὴν καὶ μέσα τῶν ὄντων ἁπάντων ἔχων εὐθείᾳ περαίνει κατὰ φύσιν περιπορευόμενος· τῷ δ᾿ ἀεὶ ξυνέπεται δίκη τῶν ἀπολελειμμένων τοῦ θείου νόμου τιμωρὸς, ἧς ὁ μὲν εὐδαιμονήσειν μέλλων ἐχόμενος ξυνέπεται ταπεινὸς καὶ κεκοσμημένος“· οὐχ ὁρῶν ὅτι παρὰ τοῖς πολὺ Πλάτωνος ἀρχαιοτέροις λέλεκται ἐν εὐχῇ τό· „κύριε, οὐχ ὑψώθη μου ἡ καρδία, οὐδὲ ἐμετεωρίσθησαν οἱ ὀφθαλμοί μου, οὐδὲ ἐπορεύθην ἐν μεγάλοις οὐδὲ ἐν θαυμασίοις ὑπὲρ ἐμὲ, εἰ μὴ ἐταπεινοφρόνουν.“ ἅμα δὲ δηλοῦται διὰ τούτων ὅτι οὐ πάντως ὁ ταπεινοφρονῶν ἀσχημόνως καὶ ἀπαισίως ταπεινοῦται, χαμαιπετὴς ἐπὶ τῶν γονάτων καὶ πρηνὴς ἐῤῥιμμένος. ἐσθῆτα δυστήνων ἀμφισκόμενος καὶ κόνιν ἐπαμώμενος. ὁ γὰρ κατὰ τὸν προφήτην ταπεινοφρονῶν, πορευόμενος „ἐν μεγάλοις καὶ θαυμασίοις“ τοῖς ὑπὲρ αὐτὸν, τοῖς ἀληθῶς „μεγάλοις“ δόγμασι καὶ τοῖς „θαυμασίοις“ νοήμασι, ταπεινοῖ ἑαυτὸν „ὑπὸ τὴν κραταιὰν χεῖρα τοῦ θεοῦ.“ εἰ δέ τινες διὰ τὴν ἰδιωτείαν μὴ τρανώσαντες τὸ περὶ τῆς ταπεινοφροσύνης δόγμα τοιαῦτα ποιοῦσιν, οὐ τὸν λόγον αἰτιατέον, ἀλλὰ τῇ ἰδιωτείᾳ τῶν προθεμένων μὲν τὰ κρείττονα διὰ δὲ τὸν ἰδιωτισμὸν ἀποτυγχανόντων συγγνωστέον. μᾶλλον γὰρ τοῦ κατὰ Πλάτωνα ταπεινοῦ καὶ κεκοσμημένου „ταπεινὸς καὶ κεκοσμημένος“ ἐστὶν ὁ κεκοσμημένος μὲν διὰ τὸ πορεύεσθαι „ἐν μεγάλοις“ καὶ „θαυμασίοις“ ὑπὲρ αὐτόν· ταπεινὸς δὲ, ἐπεὶ καὶ ἐν τούτοις ὢν ταπεινοῦται ἑκὼν. οὐχ ὑπὸ τὸν τυχόντα ἀλλ᾿ „ὑπὸ τὴν κραταιὰν χεῖρα τοῦ θεοῦ,“ διὰ τοῦ διδασκάλου τῶν τοιούτων μαθημάτων Ἰησοῦ· „ὃς“ „οὐχ ἁρπαγμὸν ἡγήσατο εἶναι ἴσα θεῷ, ἀλλ᾿ ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσε μορφὴν δούλου λαβὼν,“ „καὶ σχήματι εὑρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρωπος ἐταπείνωσεν ἑαυτὸν, γενόμενος ὑπήκοος μέχρι θανάτου, θανάτου δὲ σταυροῦ.“ καὶ οὕτω μέγα δόγμα τὸ περὶ ταπεινοφροσύνης ἐστὶν, ὡς μὴ τὸν τυχόντα διδάσκαλον ἔχειν περὶ αὐτοῦ, ἀλλ᾿ αὐτὸν λέγειν τὸν τηλικοῦτον ἡμῶν σωτῆρα· „μάθετε ἀπ᾿ ἐμοῦ, ὅτι πρᾷός εἰμι καὶ ταπεινὸς τῇ καρδίᾳ. καὶ εὑρήσετε ἀνάπαυσιν ταῖς ψυχαῖς ὑμῶν.“
pass_a_gloss: Then after these Celsus, as having had echoed around him (περιηχηθείς) the things about humility (ταπεινοφροσύνη) and not having understood (νοήσας) it carefully (ἐπιμελῶς), wishes to speak ill of (κακολογεῖν) the [humility] among us, and thinks it a mishearing (παράκουσμα) of Plato's words, who says somewhere in the Laws: 'God (ὁ θεός), as also the ancient account (ὁ παλαιὸς λόγος), holding beginning (ἀρχή) and end (τελευτή) and middle of all beings, accomplishes (περαίνει) by a straight [path] (εὐθείᾳ) going round (περιπορευόμενος) according to nature (κατὰ φύσιν); and with him always follows Justice (δίκη), avenger (τιμωρός) of those falling short (ἀπολελειμμένων) of the divine law (θεῖος νόμος), holding to whom (ἧς ἐχόμενος) the one about to be happy (εὐδαιμονήσειν) follows humble (ταπεινός) and orderly/adorned (κεκοσμημένος)'; not seeing that among those much older than Plato was said in prayer (εὐχή): 'Lord, my heart was not lifted up (ὑψώθη), nor were my eyes raised aloft (ἐμετεωρίσθησαν), nor did I walk (ἐπορεύθην) in great things nor in wonderful things (θαυμάσια) above me, unless (εἰ μή) I was humble-minded (ἐταπεινοφρόνουν).' At the same time it is shown through these that not necessarily (οὐ πάντως) is the humble-minded humbled (ταπεινοῦται) unseemly (ἀσχημόνως) and ill-omenedly (ἀπαισίως), falling to the ground (χαμαιπετής) on the knees and flung (ἐρριμμένος) face down (πρηνής), putting on (ἀμφισκόμενος) clothing of the wretched (δύστηνοι) and heaping (ἐπαμώμενος) dust (κόνις). For the one humble-minded according to the prophet, walking 'in great and wonderful things' above him, the truly 'great' doctrines (δόγματα) and 'wonderful' thoughts (νοήματα), humbles himself 'under the mighty hand (κραταιὰ χείρ) of God.' But if some, through lack of learning (ἰδιωτεία), not having made clear (τρανώσαντες) the doctrine about humility, do such things, the word/teaching (λόγος) is not to be blamed (αἰτιατέον), but the lack of learning of those who set before themselves (προθεμένων) the better things but through simplicity (ἰδιωτισμός) fail (ἀποτυγχανόντων) is to be pardoned (συγγνωστέον). For more than the humble and orderly man according to Plato, 'humble and orderly' is he who is orderly through walking 'in great' and 'wonderful things' above him, and humble since, even being in these, he humbles himself willingly (ἑκών), not under the ordinary person (τὸν τυχόντα) but 'under the mighty hand of God', through the teacher (διδάσκαλος) of such lessons (μαθήματα), Jesus, 'who' 'did not consider (ἡγήσατο) being equal (ἴσα) to God a thing to be seized (ἁρπαγμός), but emptied (ἐκένωσε) himself taking the form (μορφή) of a slave (δοῦλος),' 'and found in fashion (σχῆμα) as a man he humbled (ἐταπείνωσεν) himself, becoming obedient (ὑπήκοος) unto death, and death of a cross (σταυρός).' And so great a doctrine is that about humility that it has no ordinary teacher about it, but our so great (τηλικοῦτος) Saviour (σωτήρ) himself says: 'learn from me, because I am gentle (πρᾷος) and humble (ταπεινός) in heart, and you will find rest (ἀνάπαυσις) for your souls.'
pass_b_english: Next, Celsus, like someone who has heard talk of humility at second hand and has not taken the trouble to understand it, wants to speak ill of the humility we teach, and thinks it a mishearing of Plato’s words. Plato says somewhere in the Laws: “God, as the ancient saying has it, holding the beginning, the end and the middle of all things that are, goes straight to his end as he moves round according to nature. And Justice always follows him, the avenger of those who fall short of the divine law; and he who is to be happy holds fast to her and follows, humble and well-ordered” (Plato, Laws 4.715e–716a). Celsus does not see that, among men far more ancient than Plato, these words were spoken in prayer: “Lord, my heart was not lifted up, nor were my eyes raised high; nor did I walk among great things, nor among wonderful things above me, unless I was humble-minded” (Psalm 131:1–2).

At the same time these words show that the humble-minded man does not necessarily humble himself in an unseemly and degrading way, falling to the ground on his knees and throwing himself face down, putting on the clothes of the wretched and heaping dust on himself. For the man who is humble-minded as the prophet describes walks “among great and wonderful things” above him (Psalm 131:1), among doctrines that are truly “great” and thoughts that are truly “wonderful,” and he humbles himself “under the mighty hand of God” (1 Peter 5:6). If some, through lack of learning, have not grasped clearly the teaching on humility and act in this way, the teaching is not to blame; rather we should pardon the lack of learning in those who have set the better things before themselves but, through their simplicity, fail to reach them.

For more truly “humble and well-ordered” than Plato’s humble and well-ordered man is the one who is well-ordered because he walks “among great” and “wonderful things” above him, and humble because, even while among these, he humbles himself of his own will, not under just anyone but “under the mighty hand of God” (1 Peter 5:6), through Jesus, the teacher of such lessons, who “did not count being equal with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave,” and “being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:6–8). So great is the teaching on humility that its teacher is no ordinary one, but our Saviour himself, great as he is, says: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29).

choices.choice: LXX renumbering: the prayer is LXX Psalm 130:1–2 = English Psalm 131:1–2; εἰ μὴ ἐταπεινοφρόνουν opens LXX 130:2. The Hebrew of 131:2 differs; Origen’s argument depends on the LXX ‘unless I was humble-minded’, read as: the humble man does walk among great things, but humbly. The Plato quotation is Laws 4.715e–716a. κεκοσμημένος is rendered ‘well-ordered’ throughout so that Origen’s play on Plato’s word stays visible; it also carries the sense ‘adorned’, which is what Origen means when he says the Christian is κεκοσμημένος because he walks among great and wonderful things. The vivid list (falling on the knees, face down, rags of the wretched, heaping dust) is in poetic diction and probably echoes Celsus’s own caricature of Christian humility, but the Greek does not attribute it here, so it is not set in quotation marks. οὐ πάντως rendered ‘not necessarily’ (it could also be read ‘by no means’); the following sentence, which admits that some simple Christians do act this way, supports ‘not necessarily’. ἀπαισίως literally ‘in an ill-omened way’, rendered ‘degrading’. ὁ λόγος in ‘the teaching is not to blame’ is taken as the Christian teaching. Philippians 2:6–8 is quoted in two pieces in the Greek (the clause ‘being made in the likeness of men’ in 2:7 is not quoted); the English keeps the two pieces as two quotations and adds nothing. δούλου rendered ‘slave’. 1 Peter 5:6 ‘under the mighty hand of God’ is cited at both uses.
